prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)  -- A roadside bombing in Somalia's capital killed 21 women who were cleaning rubbish from a southern Mogadishu street on Sunday morning, a hospital official said. Mogadishu residents gather around victims of the bomb attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road. The bomb blast wounded another 46 people, most of them Somali women who had gathered to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in southern Mogadishu's Kilometer 4 district, according to Medina Hospital director Dr. Dahir Dhere. "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area," said witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." "They were innocent poor mothers or sisters," Gedi said. "Why did they deserve this?" It is unclear who is behind the attack. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently fired by the country's prime minister, blamed the Islamic Courts Union for waging the attack. But the head of the Islamist insurgent group, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, denied any involvement and blamed Somalia's government for orchestrating the attack. The victims were participating in a program that allows Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The United Nations' World Food Program organized the program, which began last year and is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority. Mogadishu has been the site of violence in recent months between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's current transitional government is trying to maintain control of the capital, with the help of the better-equipped Ethiopian forces. On Saturday, two-thirds of the Somali government ministers announced their resignations, blaming Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," which they said included his firing of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade said he suspects the mass resignations were aimed at weakening implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He said he had no plans to resign. The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Court Union which overthrew the government in 2006. The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia's transitional government. If followed, the peace deal would pave the way for a withdrawal of Ethiopian troops -- a major sticking point for Islamist fighters who oppose their presence. The agreement calls on the alliance to dissociate itself from armed groups still fighting the government and for all sides to allow "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somalis. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will monitor the agreement's implementation. Ethiopian forces became embroiled in an Islamist insurgency after the Ethiopian forces invaded Somalia in December 2006 to overthrow the ICU leaders and reinstall the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks mounted, efforts to replace the Ethiopians with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission faltered. Ethiopia's invasion had the blessing of Somalia's government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring fugitives from the al Qaeda terrorist movement. The conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, further worsening a humanitarian crisis that dates back to the collapse of the country's last government in 1991. The situation has been exacerbated by drought, continual armed conflicts in central and southern Somalia, and high inflation on food and fuel prices. CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

The victims were taking part in a program that enables Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. Launched last year and administered by Mogadishu's regional authority, the initiative was organized by the United Nations' World Food Program.

Dr. Dahir Dhere, who directs Medina Hospital, reported that the detonation also injured 46 additional people. The majority of these victims were Somali women who had assembled to tidy up Maka Al Mukarama Road in the Kilometer 4 neighborhood of southern Mogadishu.

Asha Ise Gedi, who witnessed the event, described the horror: "In an instant, the whole place became a scene of slaughter, with pieces of the street sweepers' bodies flung across a wide stretch. Blood had collected everywhere I looked. Never before have I witnessed killing on this scale."

Gedi went on to say, "These were harmless, impoverished mothers and sisters. What had they done to earn such a fate?"

Responsibility for the bombing remains undetermined. Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, the city's mayor who was dismissed not long ago by the prime minister, pointed the finger at the Islamic Courts Union as the perpetrator. However, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, who leads the Islamist rebel faction, rejected any connection and instead accused the Somali government of engineering the bombing.

Those killed had been taking part in an initiative that permits Somali women to earn food by working as street cleaners. This program, launched the previous year, was set up by the United Nations' World Food Program and is run by Mogadishu's local government.

Over the past several months, Mogadishu has witnessed clashes between forces from Ethiopia and Islamist combatants. Somalia's transitional government—backed by the more heavily armed Ethiopian military—is attempting to hold on to control of the capital.

On the preceding Saturday, roughly two out of every three ministers in the Somali government declared they were stepping down. They pointed to what they characterized as Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," a charge that encompassed his removal of the capital's mayor.

Nur Ade responded by suggesting he believed the wave of resignations was designed to undermine the enactment of the peace accord reached between the country's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He stated that he had no intention of leaving his post.

That peace arrangement, which was inked on June 9 in Djibouti, mandates a halt to hostilities between the U.N.-supported transitional Somali government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. This opposition coalition counts among its ranks individuals from the Islamist Court Union, the group responsible for toppling the government back in 2006. Later that same year, Ethiopian troops—assisted by Somalia's transitional government—drove the ICU from power.

Should the terms be honored, the agreement would clear the path for Ethiopian forces to depart—a central point of contention for Islamist fighters who reject their presence in the country. Under the accord, the alliance must sever ties with armed factions that continue battling the government, and every party is obligated to permit "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somali people. Oversight of the deal's execution will fall to a joint committee headed by U.N. representatives.

Ethiopian troops found themselves entangled in an Islamist uprising following their December 2006 incursion into Somalia, an operation aimed at removing the ICU's leadership and restoring the transitional government to power. As rebel assaults grew more frequent, attempts to swap out the Ethiopian presence for a peacekeeping force under African Union leadership stalled.

Both Somalia's government and the United States had sanctioned Ethiopia's military action, with Washington charging that the ICU was sheltering individuals wanted in connection with the al Qaeda terrorist network.

The fighting drove hundreds of thousands of Somalis from their homes, deepening a humanitarian catastrophe with roots stretching back to the disintegration of Somalia's most recent functioning government in 1991. Drought conditions, persistent armed hostilities across central and southern regions of the country, and soaring prices for food and fuel have all intensified the crisis.

*CNN's Alan Duke, along with journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed, contributed to this report.*

# At Least 21 Killed as Roadside Bomb Strikes Street Cleaners in Mogadishu

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A powerful roadside bomb tore through a group of municipal street cleaners in the Somali capital on Tuesday, killing at least 21 women and wounding more than a dozen others in one of the deadliest attacks to hit the city in recent months, officials and witnesses said.

The blast struck as the workers, most of them women employed to sweep the city's dusty thoroughfares, gathered along a busy road in the northern part of Mogadishu during the early morning hours. Ambulances rushed the wounded to nearby hospitals, where doctors said several victims remained in critical condition.

## 'Bodies Everywhere'

Witnesses described scenes of chaos and horror in the aftermath of the explosion.

"I heard a huge blast and then saw smoke rising into the sky," said Ahmed Nur, a shopkeeper whose store sits near the site of the bombing. "When I ran to help, there were bodies everywhere. These were poor women who came here every day just to earn a little money to feed their children."

Another resident, Halima Abdi, said she lost a neighbor in the attack. "She was a mother of six. What did she do to deserve this? These women harmed no one," she said, weeping.

Hospital officials struggled to cope with the influx of casualties. "We received many wounded, and some arrived with severe injuries," said a doctor at Madina Hospital who asked not to be named. "We are doing everything we can, but our resources are limited."

## Competing Accusations

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the bombing, though suspicion quickly fell on al-Shabaab, the al Qaeda-linked militant group that has waged a years-long insurgency against Somalia's central government.

Government officials were quick to blame the militants. "This cowardly attack targeting innocent women bears the hallmarks of al-Shabaab's terrorism," a Somali security official told CNN. "They have no regard for human life, including that of the most vulnerable in our society."

Al-Shabaab has frequently used roadside bombs and suicide attacks in its campaign to topple the internationally backed government and impose its strict interpretation of Islamic law. The group has previously targeted government workers and those it accuses of collaborating with authorities.

However, the militant group did not immediately issue a statement, and some residents voiced skepticism about the official narrative, pointing to broader instability in the capital. In Somalia's fractured political landscape, clan rivalries and disputes among armed factions have also fueled violence, complicating efforts to assign blame.

## A Nation Struggling for Stability

The attack underscores the persistent insecurity that has plagued Somalia, a Horn of Africa nation that has struggled with conflict and weak central governance for decades.

Since the collapse of the last functioning national government in 1991, Somalia has endured cycles of civil war, clan warfare, and Islamist insurgency. The current federal government, supported by the international community and African Union forces, has fought to extend its authority beyond the capital, but al-Shabaab continues to control swaths of territory in the south and center of the country and retains the ability to carry out deadly attacks even in areas nominally under government control.

Street cleaners and other municipal workers have found themselves on the front lines of this violence, in part because they are seen by militants as symbols of the government's presence in the city.

## Ethiopian Involvement

The bombing also comes against the backdrop of Ethiopia's long and controversial role in Somali affairs. Ethiopian troops first entered Somalia in force in 2006, when they intervened to oust an Islamist movement that had briefly seized control of Mogadishu. That intervention, backed at the time by the United States, drew fierce resentment from many Somalis and is widely seen as having fueled the rise of al-Shabaab, which emerged from the more radical wing of the ousted movement.

Ethiopian forces have since operated in Somalia at various times, both unilaterally and as part of the African Union peacekeeping mission. Their presence remains a source of tension, with al-Shabaab frequently invoking the specter of "foreign occupation" in its propaganda to rally support and justify its attacks.

Relations between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu have at times been strained over the terms and scope of Ethiopian military involvement, adding another layer of complexity to the region's security dynamics.

## Calls for Justice

Somali officials pledged to investigate the bombing and bring those responsible to justice.

"We will not allow terrorists to break the spirit of our people," the security official said. "These women were serving their city, and their deaths will not be in vain."

As night fell over Mogadishu, families gathered to mourn and prepare for burials in accordance with Islamic tradition. For many residents, the attack was a grim reminder of the fragility of daily life in a city still scarred by conflict.

"We just want to live in peace," said Nur, the shopkeeper. "Is that too much to ask?"

# Bombing at UN Food-for-Work Site Kills Women in Mogadishu Amid Deepening Political Crisis

**MOGADISHU** — A roadside bombing struck a group of women participating in a United Nations food-for-work program in the Somali capital, killing several and wounding others as they cleared debris from a Mogadishu street, humanitarian officials and witnesses said.

The women had been taking part in a World Food Program (WFP) initiative that pays impoverished residents in food rations to clean streets and clear rubble, part of broader efforts to provide relief in a city battered by years of conflict and recurrent drought.

Witnesses described a scene of chaos following the blast, with bodies and debris scattered across the roadway. Rescuers and fellow workers rushed to carry the wounded to nearby hospitals, several of which have struggled with shortages of medical supplies and personnel.

"These were women trying to earn food for their families through honest labor," said one aid official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media. "They posed no threat to anyone. This is an attack on the most vulnerable people we serve."

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the bombing. Such attacks have frequently been blamed on militants opposed to both the internationally backed government and the presence of foreign aid organizations, which insurgents have accused of advancing outside agendas.

## Aid Operations Under Threat

The killings underscore the extraordinary dangers facing humanitarian operations in Somalia, where relief workers and beneficiaries alike have increasingly become targets. The WFP and other agencies have periodically suspended or curtailed operations in parts of the country following threats and violence against staff and program participants.

The food-for-work schemes are designed to inject resources into the local economy while improving public infrastructure, offering an alternative to direct food handouts. But the visibility of the projects — with participants gathered in the open on city streets — can leave them exposed to attack.

Humanitarian officials warned that continued violence could force further reductions in aid at a time when large numbers of Somalis depend on outside assistance to survive. Aid groups have repeatedly called on all parties to the conflict to respect the neutrality of relief operations and protect civilians.

## Government in Turmoil

The bombing comes as Somalia's fragile transitional government grapples with mounting political instability, including a wave of resignations that has thrown the administration into disarray.

Several government ministers have stepped down in recent days, deepening a crisis that has exposed rifts within the leadership and raised questions about the government's ability to function. The departures have compounded the challenges facing an administration that already exercises limited control beyond the capital and relies heavily on outside military and financial support.

The political upheaval has fueled uncertainty at a critical moment, as authorities struggle to confront the armed insurgency, provide basic services, and maintain a semblance of order in Mogadishu.

Analysts say the combination of insurgent violence, governmental paralysis, and humanitarian emergency has created a dangerous spiral, with each crisis feeding the others. The infighting among political leaders, they note, has distracted from efforts to address security and reconstruction.

## A Beleaguered Capital

Mogadishu has endured years of factional fighting, insurgency, and lawlessness that have devastated infrastructure and displaced hundreds of thousands of residents. Ordinary civilians have borne the brunt of the violence, caught between warring parties and struggling to meet basic needs.

For the women who joined the WFP cleanup program, the work represented a rare opportunity to earn food in a city where employment is scarce and hunger widespread. Their deaths have highlighted the grim calculus facing many Somalis, for whom even efforts to survive can carry deadly risk.

International officials condemned the attack and pressed Somali authorities to bring those responsible to justice, though accountability has proven elusive in a country where the justice system, like much of the state apparatus, remains weak.

As Mogadishu residents mourned the latest victims, aid agencies faced renewed pressure to weigh the imperative of delivering assistance against the safety of those they aim to help — a dilemma that has come to define humanitarian work in one of the world's most enduring crises.

Government officials attributed the attack to Islamist insurgents who have waged a persistent campaign against the transitional administration and its allies. The insurgents have frequently employed roadside bombs and hit-and-run tactics, though no group immediately claimed responsibility for the deadly blast.

Attacks on civilians and workers seen as cooperating with the government have become a recurring feature of the conflict, deepening the sense of insecurity that pervades daily life in the capital.

## A Government Struggling to Assert Control

The transitional federal government continues to face profound difficulties in establishing authority over Mogadishu and the broader country. Despite international recognition, the administration has struggled to provide basic security, deliver services, or extend its reach beyond limited areas of the capital.

The persistent violence underscores the fragility of a government that many Somalis view as unable to protect them.

## Ethiopian Troops in the Mix

Complicating the situation is the presence of Ethiopian troops, who intervened to support the transitional government against insurgent forces. Their deployment has proven deeply divisive, with many Somalis resentful of the foreign military presence.

Rather than stabilizing the country, the intervention has in many respects fueled further resistance and become a rallying point for insurgent recruitment, adding another volatile dimension to an already complex conflict.

## Decades of Suffering

Somalia has endured relentless turmoil since 1991, when the collapse of the central government plunged the nation into civil war and clan-based fighting. In the years since, the country has lacked a functioning national authority, and generations of Somalis have grown up knowing only conflict.

The humanitarian consequences have been staggering. Hundreds of thousands have died from violence, famine, and disease, while countless others have been displaced within the country or forced to flee abroad. Aid organizations have repeatedly warned of dire conditions, with civilians bearing the heaviest burden of the unending crisis.

Wednesday's bombing, claiming the lives of workers simply trying to clean the city's streets, stands as a grim reminder of how ordinary Somalis continue to pay the price for a conflict with no clear end in sight.

# Deadly Bombing Rocks Mogadishu as Political Crisis Deepens

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A powerful explosion tore through a crowded district of the Somali capital, killing dozens and wounding scores more in one of the deadliest attacks to strike the volatile city in recent memory. The blast has intensified an already-simmering political crisis, sparking bitter recriminations between government officials and Islamist factions while accelerating a wave of ministerial resignations.

## The Attack

The bombing struck during peak hours, when markets and streets were densely packed with civilians. Hospital officials reported that the casualty count climbed steadily throughout the day as rescue workers pulled bodies from the rubble and treated the wounded, many suffering from severe shrapnel injuries and burns. Overwhelmed medical facilities struggled to cope with the influx, and doctors warned that the death toll could rise further given the number of critically injured patients.

Witnesses described scenes of devastation—collapsed structures, burning vehicles, and desperate relatives searching for missing family members amid the chaos.

## The Blame Game

In the aftermath, responsibility for the attack became a point of fierce political contention. The mayor of Mogadishu pointed an accusatory finger directly at the Islamic Courts Union (ICU), the Islamist movement that once controlled much of southern Somalia. He characterized the bombing as part of a coordinated insurgent campaign designed to destabilize the fragile transitional government and terrorize the civilian population.

The Islamic Courts Union, for its part, denied involvement and rejected the mayor's characterization. ICU representatives dismissed the allegations as political opportunism, suggesting the government was exploiting the tragedy to justify its own hardline policies and deflect attention from its internal failures.

## Government in Turmoil

The bombing unfolded against the backdrop of a deepening rift within the transitional government itself. Several Somali ministers announced their resignations, citing what they described as the prime minister's increasingly autocratic style of governance. The departing officials accused the premier of concentrating power, sidelining cabinet colleagues, and ruling in a manner they characterized as dictatorial.

The resignations exposed profound fractures within the administration, raising questions about its ability to govern effectively at a moment when unity was most needed. Critics argued that the internal dysfunction only emboldened insurgent groups and further eroded public confidence in a government already struggling to establish legitimate authority.

## The Ethiopian Shadow

To understand the current instability, observers point to the pivotal events of late 2006. That year, Ethiopian military forces launched a major invasion of Somalia, intervening to support the internationally recognized Transitional Federal Government against the rapidly expanding Islamic Courts Union.

The ICU had, over the preceding months, seized control of Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia, imposing a degree of order that had eluded the country since the collapse of central government in 1991. Neighboring Ethiopia, however, viewed the Islamist movement as a security threat—concerned both about the ICU's ties to armed groups and about irredentist claims on Ethiopian territory in the Ogaden region.

The Ethiopian offensive quickly routed ICU forces and drove them from the capital. Yet the intervention, far from stabilizing the country, ignited a fierce insurgency. Many Somalis regarded the Ethiopian presence as a foreign occupation, and the ICU's remnants—along with more radical splinter factions—regrouped to wage a guerrilla campaign against both Ethiopian troops and the government they propped up.

The bombing represents the latest chapter in this ongoing conflict, a grim reminder that the wounds opened by the 2006 invasion remain far from healed. As the government fractures from within and insurgents press their campaign from without, ordinary Somalis continue to bear the heaviest cost.
